To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the development of a broad-spectrum HPV vaccine is feasible, but will require a combination of different strategies.
L2-based HPV vaccines have been developed, and that they have been found to be effective against a broad spectrum of HPV types.
L2-based HPV vaccines induce broadly cross-neutralizing and protective immunity against heterologous HPV types in animal challenge models.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of L2-based vaccines that are more effective than current L1-VLP prophylactic vaccines, and that provide broader protection against mucosal and cutaneous HPVs, as well as against betaPV types causing NMSC.
the development of a new generation of L2-based HPV vaccines that will be more efficacious and will protect against a broader spectrum of HPV types than the currently licensed L1-VLP HPV vaccines.
the development of novel, L2-based vaccines that protect against a broad spectrum of HPV types and that can prevent HPV-associated diseases in immunocompromised individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current vaccines are not the ultimate answer, and that the development of L2-based vaccines is still in its infancy.
HPV vaccines are a success story and have been a breakthrough in prevention of cervical carcinoma and a number of other HPV-associated malignancies and benign diseases.
the L2-VLP approach is a very promising alternative for the development of a broadly effective HPV vaccine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of a multivalent vaccine against HPV types causing cervical and ano-genital cancers, as well as a vaccine against betaPV types causing NMSC is a challenging task.
L2 is an attractive candidate for the development of a broad-spectrum HPV vaccine, and we have developed a novel L2-based HPV vaccine that has shown promising results in animal models.
we are now able to generate broadly cross-neutralizing anti-HPV L2 antibodies that are able to protect against infection with heterologous HPV types.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immunogenicity of HPV L2 (poly)peptides can be significantly improved by using a combination of different approaches.
L2-based vaccine candidates can induce broadly cross-neutralizing antibody titers in humans.
L2 (poly)peptide vaccines are promising candidates to provide broad protection against HPV types causing benign and oncogenic mucosal and cutaneous lesions.
